frameworks.name: ROIC Decision Framework
frameworks.definition: Evaluating scaling decisions by calculating return on invested capital per new location: investment cost + recruitment cost compared to annual profit generated at payoff timeline.

frameworks.name: Capital Redeployment Trade-off
frameworks.definition: The explicit choice between retaining profit for security (no growth) versus redeploying cash for growth (higher risk, higher upside).

claims.text: At $25M annual revenue with 21% EBITDA, the dental practice owner has sufficient internally generated cash flow (approximately $5.25M in profits) to self-fund de novo office openings at $250-300K per location plus $100K in team recruitment costs, without external capital.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with documented unit economics
bounded_by: Does not account for working capital requirements beyond the stated investment
Assumes consistent recruitment costs as the organization scales

claims.text: De novo dental practice locations achieve 12-18 month payback on the $350-400K total investment (location + team recruitment), returning $500K+ in profit annually once stabilized, representing 1.4x+ ROIC within 18 months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: payback timeline and ROIC on per-location investment

bounded_by: Payback timeline assumes stable profitability achievement
Does not account for operator error or failed locations

claims.text: At the growth velocity required ($5-6M in new office revenue annually, equivalent to 2-3 new de novo locations per year), the limiting constraint is not capital availability but rather talent acquisition velocity—specifically sourcing qualified dentists and treatment coordinators at the rate growth demands.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Capital constraint is overcome by profit redeployment (profitable business can self-fund growth); talent constraint cannot be outsourced to lending sources. Dentist hiring is the core economic engine and becomes harder at scale despite podcast and community network sourcing.

anchors.value: 6 dentists per year, plus 4-5 staff per location = ~1 hire every 2 weeks
Dental podcast + partner community network (informal, not systematized)

bounded_by: Sourcing difficulty is self-reported; no data on actual fill rates or time-to-hire by role

claims.text: A dedicated talent acquisition specialist (or small recruiting firm retained exclusively for core repeating roles) generates sufficient ROI to justify the cost when hiring velocity exceeds approximately one role every two weeks, because the reduction in time-to-fill directly compounds growth velocity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Role is core to economic engine
claims.mechanism: Systematic recruiting process (sourcing, screening, offer negotiation) for core roles compounds more than outsourcing to generalist headhunters. Dedicated resource eliminates ad hoc hiring delays.
bounded_by: Does not apply to one-time specialist hires (CFO, outside counsel) where headhunter networks have existing relationships
Assumes the organization has documented hiring criteria and onboarding processes

claims.text: Profit redeployment (trading profit retention for growth) and talent velocity (hiring dedicated recruiting resources) are mathematically equivalent trade-off equations: both convert a known constraint (cash or time) into the ability to scale one additional office per period.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with repeatable unit economics
Growth constrained by two levers simultaneously
bounded_by: Assumes both capital and talent decisions are discretionary (not externally forced)
The analogy breaks if one constraint is genuinely non-fungible

claims.text: Dental practices fail to scale past 1 office per year (instead of the target 2-3) because founder/owner is perceived as bearing hiring and capital risk personally, rather than evaluating growth as a capital allocation problem with measurable ROIC.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Owner has described capital constraint but has actual cash available
claims.mechanism: Emotional/mental constraint (fear of deploying capital, preference for external funding) overrides rational ROIC math. Owner frames self-funding as 'more risky' because bank debt feels externalized.
bounded_by: The owner disputes this during conversation ('it feels less risky to use someone's money'), indicating the constraint may be partially real (bank paused funding) rather than purely psychological

examples.text: The dental practice owner operates 10 de novo offices across Florida, generating $25M in annual revenue with 21% EBITDA ($5.25M in profit). Each office costs $250-300K to open (second-gen space + equipment), plus ~$100K for team recruitment. Year 1 offices typically produce $1.5M in revenue at lower margins. Once stabilized, offices reach $2.5M revenue at 20%+ EBITDA margins ($500K+ profit), achieving full ROI in 12-18 months. The business is profitable enough to self-fund growth at 2-3 new offices annually (using 25% of profits) but the owner is uncertain whether to deploy internal capital or wait for bank funding.

The owner sources dentists and staff through a dental podcast and a partner's deep community network connections. As the business scales from 1 office per year to 2-3 offices per year, this informal sourcing channel becomes insufficient. The hiring velocity jumps to approximately one role every two weeks (6 dentists per year + 4-5 staff per location), yet the informal podcast/network sourcing cannot fill roles at that rate. This illustrates the transition from ad hoc to systematic hiring as a growth constraint.

practices.text: Deploy 20-25% of annual profits into de novo location expansion rather than retaining all profit as owner distributions. At $5.25M annual profit, allocating $1.3M annually enables 3-4 new locations per year with high confidence of payback within 18 months.

Establish a dedicated internal recruiting resource (or retainer firm) focused exclusively on filling core, repeating roles (dentists, patient care coordinators, regional managers) once hiring velocity exceeds one role per two weeks. Avoid distributing recruiting effort across general headhunters unless the role is one-time specialized hiring (CFO, legal counsel).

Separate the recruitment of specialized, one-time roles (e.g., regional manager) from the recruitment of core, repeating roles (dentists, staff). Use headhunter networks for one-time positions where existing networks save time. Build internal recruiting processes for roles that appear repeatedly as the business scales.
